func_details.relevant_paper:
Energy Pointing Game (EPG) measures the concentration of attribution energy within the mask, the
fraction of positive attributions inside the bounding boxes:
$$\label{eq:epg}
    \text{EPG}_k = \frac{\sum_{h=1}^H\sum_{w=1}^W M_{k,hw} A^+_{k,hw}}{\sum_{h=1}^H\sum_{w=1}^W A^+_{k,hw}}\;.$$

In addition to
the losses described in prior work, we propose to also evaluate using
the score (, [\[eq:epg\]](#eq:epg){reference-type="ref"
reference="eq:epg"}) as a loss function for model guidance, as it is
fully differentiable. In particular, we simply define it as
$$\label{eq:energyloss}
\textstyle
    \mathcal{L}_{\text{loc},k} = -\text{EPG}_k.$$ Unlike existing
localization losses that either (i) do not constrain attributions across
the entire input (, ), or (ii) force the model to attribute uniformly
within the mask even if it includes irrelevant background regions (, ),
maximizing the score jointly optimizes for higher attribution energy
within the mask and lower attribution energy outside the mask. By not
enforcing a uniformity prior, we find that the loss is able to provide
effective guidance while allowing the model to learn freely what to
focus on within the bounding boxes

func_details.relevant_paper:
Energy Pointing Game (EPG) measures the concentration of attribution energy within the mask, the
fraction of positive attributions inside the bounding boxes:
$$\label{eq:epg}
    \text{EPG}_k = \frac{\sum_{h=1}^H\sum_{w=1}^W M_{k,hw} A^+_{k,hw}}{\sum_{h=1}^H\sum_{w=1}^W A^+_{k,hw}}\;.$$

In addition to
the losses described in prior work, we propose to also evaluate using
the score (, [\[eq:epg\]](#eq:epg){reference-type="ref"
reference="eq:epg"}) as a loss function for model guidance, as it is
fully differentiable. In particular, we simply define it as
$$\label{eq:energyloss}
\textstyle
    \mathcal{L}_{\text{loc},k} = -\text{EPG}_k.$$ Unlike existing
localization losses that either (i) do not constrain attributions across
the entire input (, ), or (ii) force the model to attribute uniformly
within the mask even if it includes irrelevant background regions (, ),
maximizing the score jointly optimizes for higher attribution energy
within the mask and lower attribution energy outside the mask. By not
enforcing a uniformity prior, we find that the loss is able to provide
effective guidance while allowing the model to learn freely what to
focus on within the bounding boxes

Energy Pointing Game (EPG) measures the concentration of attribution energy within the mask, the
fraction of positive attributions inside the bounding boxes:
$$\label{eq:epg}
    \text{EPG}_k = \frac{\sum_{h=1}^H\sum_{w=1}^W M_{k,hw} A^+_{k,hw}}{\sum_{h=1}^H\sum_{w=1}^W A^+_{k,hw}}\;.$$

In addition to
the losses described in prior work, we propose to also evaluate using
the score (, [\[eq:epg\]](#eq:epg){reference-type="ref"
reference="eq:epg"}) as a loss function for model guidance, as it is
fully differentiable. In particular, we simply define it as
$$\label{eq:energyloss}
\textstyle
    \mathcal{L}_{\text{loc},k} = -\text{EPG}_k.$$ Unlike existing
localization losses that either (i) do not constrain attributions across
the entire input (, ), or (ii) force the model to attribute uniformly
within the mask even if it includes irrelevant background regions (, ),
maximizing the score jointly optimizes for higher attribution energy
within the mask and lower attribution energy outside the mask. By not
enforcing a uniformity prior, we find that the loss is able to provide
effective guidance while allowing the model to learn freely what to
focus on within the bounding boxes

func_details.relevant_paper:
B-cos attributions are generated using the inherently-interpretable networks,
which promote alignment between the input $\mathbf x$ and a dynamic
weight matrix $\mathbf W(\mathbf x)$ during optimization. In our
experiments, we use the contribution maps given by the element-wise
product of the dynamic weights with the input
($\mathbf W^T_k(\mathbf x)\odot \mathbf x$), which faithfully represent
the contribution of each pixel to class $k$. To be able to guide models,
we developed a differentiable implementation of explanations, see
supplement.

func_details.name: __call__
func_details.relevant_paper:
Energy Pointing Game (EPG) measures the concentration of attribution energy within the mask, the
fraction of positive attributions inside the bounding boxes:
$$\label{eq:epg}
    \text{EPG}_k = \frac{\sum_{h=1}^H\sum_{w=1}^W M_{k,hw} A^+_{k,hw}}{\sum_{h=1}^H\sum_{w=1}^W A^+_{k,hw}}\;.$$

In addition to
the losses described in prior work, we propose to also evaluate using
the score (, [\[eq:epg\]](#eq:epg){reference-type="ref"
reference="eq:epg"}) as a loss function for model guidance, as it is
fully differentiable. In particular, we simply define it as
$$\label{eq:energyloss}
\textstyle
    \mathcal{L}_{\text{loc},k} = -\text{EPG}_k.$$ Unlike existing
localization losses that either (i) do not constrain attributions across
the entire input (, ), or (ii) force the model to attribute uniformly
within the mask even if it includes irrelevant background regions (, ),
maximizing the score jointly optimizes for higher attribution energy
within the mask and lower attribution energy outside the mask. By not
enforcing a uniformity prior, we find that the loss is able to provide
effective guidance while allowing the model to learn freely what to
focus on within the bounding boxes

func_details.relevant_paper:
IxG computes the element-wise product $\odot$ of the input and the gradients
of the $k$-th output w.r.t. the input, $X\odot\nabla_X f_k(X)$. For
piece-wise linear models such as DNNs with ReLU activations , this
faithfully computes the linear contributions of a given input pixel to
the model output.

    def apply_post_processing(self, attributions):
        """
        Applies post-processing steps to attributions
        
        Post processing steps:
          - Keeping only positive values
          - Binarization
          - Interpolation

        Args:
        attributions (tensor): Computed attributions

        Returns:
        tensor: Post-processed attributions
        """
        attributions = self.check_only_positive(attributions)
        attributions = self.check_binarize(attributions)
        attributions = self.check_interpolate(attributions)
        return attributions

func_details.name: _call_batch_mode
func_details.relevant_paper:
B-cos attributions are generated using the inherently-interpretable networks,
which promote alignment between the input $\mathbf x$ and a dynamic
weight matrix $\mathbf W(\mathbf x)$ during optimization. In our
experiments, we use the contribution maps given by the element-wise
product of the dynamic weights with the input
($\mathbf W^T_k(\mathbf x)\odot \mathbf x$), which faithfully represent
the contribution of each pixel to class $k$. To be able to guide models,
we developed a differentiable implementation of explanations, see
supplement.

func_details.relevant_paper:
Energy Pointing Game (EPG) measures the concentration of attribution energy within the mask, the
fraction of positive attributions inside the bounding boxes:
$$\label{eq:epg}
    \text{EPG}_k = \frac{\sum_{h=1}^H\sum_{w=1}^W M_{k,hw} A^+_{k,hw}}{\sum_{h=1}^H\sum_{w=1}^W A^+_{k,hw}}\;.$$

In addition to
the losses described in prior work, we propose to also evaluate using
the score (, [\[eq:epg\]](#eq:epg){reference-type="ref"
reference="eq:epg"}) as a loss function for model guidance, as it is
fully differentiable. In particular, we simply define it as
$$\label{eq:energyloss}
\textstyle
    \mathcal{L}_{\text{loc},k} = -\text{EPG}_k.$$ Unlike existing
localization losses that either (i) do not constrain attributions across
the entire input (, ), or (ii) force the model to attribute uniformly
within the mask even if it includes irrelevant background regions (, ),
maximizing the score jointly optimizes for higher attribution energy
within the mask and lower attribution energy outside the mask. By not
enforcing a uniformity prior, we find that the loss is able to provide
effective guidance while allowing the model to learn freely what to
focus on within the bounding boxes

Energy Pointing Game (EPG) measures the concentration of attribution energy within the mask, the
fraction of positive attributions inside the bounding boxes:
$$\label{eq:epg}
    \text{EPG}_k = \frac{\sum_{h=1}^H\sum_{w=1}^W M_{k,hw} A^+_{k,hw}}{\sum_{h=1}^H\sum_{w=1}^W A^+_{k,hw}}\;.$$

In addition to
the losses described in prior work, we propose to also evaluate using
the score (, [\[eq:epg\]](#eq:epg){reference-type="ref"
reference="eq:epg"}) as a loss function for model guidance, as it is
fully differentiable. In particular, we simply define it as
$$\label{eq:energyloss}
\textstyle
    \mathcal{L}_{\text{loc},k} = -\text{EPG}_k.$$ Unlike existing
localization losses that either (i) do not constrain attributions across
the entire input (, ), or (ii) force the model to attribute uniformly
within the mask even if it includes irrelevant background regions (, ),
maximizing the score jointly optimizes for higher attribution energy
within the mask and lower attribution energy outside the mask. By not
enforcing a uniformity prior, we find that the loss is able to provide
effective guidance while allowing the model to learn freely what to
focus on within the bounding boxes

gradient-weighted sum of activation maps. In detail, it is given by
$\text{ReLU}(\sum_c \alpha_c^k \odot U_c)$ with $c$ denoting the channel
dimension, and $\alpha^k$ the average-pooled gradients of the output for
class $k$ with respect to the activations $U$ of the last convolutional
layer in the model.

$$\label{eq:epg}
    \text{EPG}_k = \frac{\sum_{h=1}^H\sum_{w=1}^W M_{k,hw} A^+_{k,hw}}{\sum_{h=1}^H\sum_{w=1}^W A^+_{k,hw}}\;.$$

In addition to
the losses described in prior work, we propose to also evaluate using
the score (, [\[eq:epg\]](#eq:epg){reference-type="ref"
reference="eq:epg"}) as a loss function for model guidance, as it is
fully differentiable. In particular, we simply define it as
$$\label{eq:energyloss}
\textstyle
    \mathcal{L}_{\text{loc},k} = -\text{EPG}_k.$$ Unlike existing
localization losses that either (i) do not constrain attributions across
the entire input (, ), or (ii) force the model to attribute uniformly
within the mask even if it includes irrelevant background regions (, ),
maximizing the score jointly optimizes for higher attribution energy
within the mask and lower attribution energy outside the mask. By not
enforcing a uniformity prior, we find that the loss is able to provide
effective guidance while allowing the model to learn freely what to
focus on within the bounding boxes

func_details.relevant_paper:
B-cos attributions are generated using the inherently-interpretable networks,
which promote alignment between the input $\mathbf x$ and a dynamic
weight matrix $\mathbf W(\mathbf x)$ during optimization. In our
experiments, we use the contribution maps given by the element-wise
product of the dynamic weights with the input
($\mathbf W^T_k(\mathbf x)\odot \mathbf x$), which faithfully represent
the contribution of each pixel to class $k$. To be able to guide models,
we developed a differentiable implementation of explanations, see
supplement.

func_details.relevant_paper:
Energy Pointing Game (EPG) measures the concentration of attribution energy within the mask, the
fraction of positive attributions inside the bounding boxes:
$$\label{eq:epg}
    \text{EPG}_k = \frac{\sum_{h=1}^H\sum_{w=1}^W M_{k,hw} A^+_{k,hw}}{\sum_{h=1}^H\sum_{w=1}^W A^+_{k,hw}}\;.$$

In addition to
the losses described in prior work, we propose to also evaluate using
the score (, [\[eq:epg\]](#eq:epg){reference-type="ref"
reference="eq:epg"}) as a loss function for model guidance, as it is
fully differentiable. In particular, we simply define it as
$$\label{eq:energyloss}
\textstyle
    \mathcal{L}_{\text{loc},k} = -\text{EPG}_k.$$ Unlike existing
localization losses that either (i) do not constrain attributions across
the entire input (, ), or (ii) force the model to attribute uniformly
within the mask even if it includes irrelevant background regions (, ),
maximizing the score jointly optimizes for higher attribution energy
within the mask and lower attribution energy outside the mask. By not
enforcing a uniformity prior, we find that the loss is able to provide
effective guidance while allowing the model to learn freely what to
focus on within the bounding boxes

func_details.relevant_paper:
Energy Pointing Game (EPG) measures the concentration of attribution energy within the mask, the
fraction of positive attributions inside the bounding boxes:
$$\label{eq:epg}
    \text{EPG}_k = \frac{\sum_{h=1}^H\sum_{w=1}^W M_{k,hw} A^+_{k,hw}}{\sum_{h=1}^H\sum_{w=1}^W A^+_{k,hw}}\;.$$

In addition to
the losses described in prior work, we propose to also evaluate using
the score (, [\[eq:epg\]](#eq:epg){reference-type="ref"
reference="eq:epg"}) as a loss function for model guidance, as it is
fully differentiable. In particular, we simply define it as
$$\label{eq:energyloss}
\textstyle
    \mathcal{L}_{\text{loc},k} = -\text{EPG}_k.$$ Unlike existing
localization losses that either (i) do not constrain attributions across
the entire input (, ), or (ii) force the model to attribute uniformly
within the mask even if it includes irrelevant background regions (, ),
maximizing the score jointly optimizes for higher attribution energy
within the mask and lower attribution energy outside the mask. By not
enforcing a uniformity prior, we find that the loss is able to provide
effective guidance while allowing the model to learn freely what to
focus on within the bounding boxes

B-cos attributions are generated using the inherently-interpretable networks,
which promote alignment between the input $\mathbf x$ and a dynamic
weight matrix $\mathbf W(\mathbf x)$ during optimization. In our
experiments, we use the contribution maps given by the element-wise
product of the dynamic weights with the input
($\mathbf W^T_k(\mathbf x)\odot \mathbf x$), which faithfully represent

we developed a differentiable implementation of explanations, see
supplement.

GradCam computes importance attributions as a ReLU-thresholded,
gradient-weighted sum of activation maps. In detail, it is given by
$\text{ReLU}(\sum_c \alpha_c^k \odot U_c)$ with $c$ denoting the channel
dimension, and $\alpha^k$ the average-pooled gradients of the output for
class $k$ with respect to the activations $U$ of the last convolutional
layer in the model.

$\text{ReLU}(\sum_c \alpha_c^k \odot U_c)$ with $c$ denoting the channel
dimension, and $\alpha^k$ the average-pooled gradients of the output for
class $k$ with respect to the activations $U$ of the last convolutional
layer in the model.

func_details.relevant_paper:
Energy Pointing Game (EPG) measures the concentration of attribution energy within the mask, the
fraction of positive attributions inside the bounding boxes:
$$\label{eq:epg}
    \text{EPG}_k = \frac{\sum_{h=1}^H\sum_{w=1}^W M_{k,hw} A^+_{k,hw}}{\sum_{h=1}^H\sum_{w=1}^W A^+_{k,hw}}\;.$$

In addition to
the losses described in prior work, we propose to also evaluate using
the score (, [\[eq:epg\]](#eq:epg){reference-type="ref"
reference="eq:epg"}) as a loss function for model guidance, as it is
fully differentiable. In particular, we simply define it as
$$\label{eq:energyloss}
\textstyle
    \mathcal{L}_{\text{loc},k} = -\text{EPG}_k.$$ Unlike existing
localization losses that either (i) do not constrain attributions across
the entire input (, ), or (ii) force the model to attribute uniformly
within the mask even if it includes irrelevant background regions (, ),
maximizing the score jointly optimizes for higher attribution energy
within the mask and lower attribution energy outside the mask. By not
enforcing a uniformity prior, we find that the loss is able to provide
effective guidance while allowing the model to learn freely what to
focus on within the bounding boxes

func_details.relevant_paper:
B-cos attributions are generated using the inherently-interpretable networks,
which promote alignment between the input $\mathbf x$ and a dynamic
weight matrix $\mathbf W(\mathbf x)$ during optimization. In our
experiments, we use the contribution maps given by the element-wise
product of the dynamic weights with the input
($\mathbf W^T_k(\mathbf x)\odot \mathbf x$), which faithfully represent
the contribution of each pixel to class $k$. To be able to guide models,
we developed a differentiable implementation of explanations, see
supplement.

func_details.relevant_paper:
Energy Pointing Game (EPG) measures the concentration of attribution energy within the mask, the
fraction of positive attributions inside the bounding boxes:
$$\label{eq:epg}
    \text{EPG}_k = \frac{\sum_{h=1}^H\sum_{w=1}^W M_{k,hw} A^+_{k,hw}}{\sum_{h=1}^H\sum_{w=1}^W A^+_{k,hw}}\;.$$

In addition to
the losses described in prior work, we propose to also evaluate using
the score (, [\[eq:epg\]](#eq:epg){reference-type="ref"
reference="eq:epg"}) as a loss function for model guidance, as it is
fully differentiable. In particular, we simply define it as
$$\label{eq:energyloss}
\textstyle
    \mathcal{L}_{\text{loc},k} = -\text{EPG}_k.$$ Unlike existing
localization losses that either (i) do not constrain attributions across
the entire input (, ), or (ii) force the model to attribute uniformly
within the mask even if it includes irrelevant background regions (, ),
maximizing the score jointly optimizes for higher attribution energy
within the mask and lower attribution energy outside the mask. By not
enforcing a uniformity prior, we find that the loss is able to provide
effective guidance while allowing the model to learn freely what to
focus on within the bounding boxes

which promote alignment between the input $\mathbf x$ and a dynamic
weight matrix $\mathbf W(\mathbf x)$ during optimization. In our
experiments, we use the contribution maps given by the element-wise
product of the dynamic weights with the input
($\mathbf W^T_k(\mathbf x)\odot \mathbf x$), which faithfully represent
the contribution of each pixel to class $k$. To be able to guide models,
we developed a differentiable implementation of explanations, see
supplement.

func_details.relevant_paper:
Energy Pointing Game (EPG) measures the concentration of attribution energy within the mask, the
fraction of positive attributions inside the bounding boxes:
$$\label{eq:epg}
    \text{EPG}_k = \frac{\sum_{h=1}^H\sum_{w=1}^W M_{k,hw} A^+_{k,hw}}{\sum_{h=1}^H\sum_{w=1}^W A^+_{k,hw}}\;.$$

In addition to
the losses described in prior work, we propose to also evaluate using
the score (, [\[eq:epg\]](#eq:epg){reference-type="ref"
reference="eq:epg"}) as a loss function for model guidance, as it is
fully differentiable. In particular, we simply define it as
$$\label{eq:energyloss}
\textstyle
    \mathcal{L}_{\text{loc},k} = -\text{EPG}_k.$$ Unlike existing
localization losses that either (i) do not constrain attributions across
the entire input (, ), or (ii) force the model to attribute uniformly
within the mask even if it includes irrelevant background regions (, ),
maximizing the score jointly optimizes for higher attribution energy
within the mask and lower attribution energy outside the mask. By not
enforcing a uniformity prior, we find that the loss is able to provide
effective guidance while allowing the model to learn freely what to
focus on within the bounding boxes

func_details.relevant_paper:
Energy Pointing Game (EPG) measures the concentration of attribution energy within the mask, the
fraction of positive attributions inside the bounding boxes:
$$\label{eq:epg}
    \text{EPG}_k = \frac{\sum_{h=1}^H\sum_{w=1}^W M_{k,hw} A^+_{k,hw}}{\sum_{h=1}^H\sum_{w=1}^W A^+_{k,hw}}\;.$$

In addition to
the losses described in prior work, we propose to also evaluate using
the score (, [\[eq:epg\]](#eq:epg){reference-type="ref"
reference="eq:epg"}) as a loss function for model guidance, as it is
fully differentiable. In particular, we simply define it as
$$\label{eq:energyloss}
\textstyle
    \mathcal{L}_{\text{loc},k} = -\text{EPG}_k.$$ Unlike existing
localization losses that either (i) do not constrain attributions across
the entire input (, ), or (ii) force the model to attribute uniformly
within the mask even if it includes irrelevant background regions (, ),
maximizing the score jointly optimizes for higher attribution energy
within the mask and lower attribution energy outside the mask. By not
enforcing a uniformity prior, we find that the loss is able to provide
effective guidance while allowing the model to learn freely what to
focus on within the bounding boxes

func_details.relevant_paper:
Energy Pointing Game (EPG) measures the concentration of attribution energy within the mask, the
fraction of positive attributions inside the bounding boxes:
$$\label{eq:epg}
    \text{EPG}_k = \frac{\sum_{h=1}^H\sum_{w=1}^W M_{k,hw} A^+_{k,hw}}{\sum_{h=1}^H\sum_{w=1}^W A^+_{k,hw}}\;.$$

In addition to
the losses described in prior work, we propose to also evaluate using
the score (, [\[eq:epg\]](#eq:epg){reference-type="ref"
reference="eq:epg"}) as a loss function for model guidance, as it is
fully differentiable. In particular, we simply define it as
$$\label{eq:energyloss}
\textstyle
    \mathcal{L}_{\text{loc},k} = -\text{EPG}_k.$$ Unlike existing
localization losses that either (i) do not constrain attributions across
the entire input (, ), or (ii) force the model to attribute uniformly
within the mask even if it includes irrelevant background regions (, ),
maximizing the score jointly optimizes for higher attribution energy
within the mask and lower attribution energy outside the mask. By not
enforcing a uniformity prior, we find that the loss is able to provide
effective guidance while allowing the model to learn freely what to
focus on within the bounding boxes

weight matrix $\mathbf W(\mathbf x)$ during optimization. In our

fraction of positive attributions inside the bounding boxes:
$$\label{eq:epg}
    \text{EPG}_k = \frac{\sum_{h=1}^H\sum_{w=1}^W M_{k,hw} A^+_{k,hw}}{\sum_{h=1}^H\sum_{w=1}^W A^+_{k,hw}}\;.$$

In addition to
the losses described in prior work, we propose to also evaluate using
the score (, [\[eq:epg\]](#eq:epg){reference-type="ref"
reference="eq:epg"}) as a loss function for model guidance, as it is
fully differentiable. In particular, we simply define it as
$$\label{eq:energyloss}
\textstyle
    \mathcal{L}_{\text{loc},k} = -\text{EPG}_k.$$ Unlike existing
localization losses that either (i) do not constrain attributions across
the entire input (, ), or (ii) force the model to attribute uniformly
within the mask even if it includes irrelevant background regions (, ),
maximizing the score jointly optimizes for higher attribution energy
within the mask and lower attribution energy outside the mask. By not
enforcing a uniformity prior, we find that the loss is able to provide
effective guidance while allowing the model to learn freely what to
focus on within the bounding boxes

func_details.relevant_paper:
B-cos attributions are generated using the inherently-interpretable networks,
which promote alignment between the input $\mathbf x$ and a dynamic
weight matrix $\mathbf W(\mathbf x)$ during optimization. In our
experiments, we use the contribution maps given by the element-wise
product of the dynamic weights with the input
($\mathbf W^T_k(\mathbf x)\odot \mathbf x$), which faithfully represent
the contribution of each pixel to class $k$. To be able to guide models,
we developed a differentiable implementation of explanations, see
supplement.

    def apply_post_processing(self, attributions):
        """
        Applies post-processing steps to attributions
        
        Post processing steps:
          - Keeping only positive values
          - Binarization
          - Interpolation

        Args:
        attributions (tensor): Computed attributions

        Returns:
        tensor: Post-processed attributions
        """
        attributions = self.check_only_positive(attributions)
        attributions = self.check_binarize(attributions)
        attributions = self.check_interpolate(attributions)
        return attributions

func_details.relevant_paper:
GradCam computes importance attributions as a ReLU-thresholded,
gradient-weighted sum of activation maps. In detail, it is given by
$\text{ReLU}(\sum_c \alpha_c^k \odot U_c)$ with $c$ denoting the channel
dimension, and $\alpha^k$ the average-pooled gradients of the output for
class $k$ with respect to the activations $U$ of the last convolutional
layer in the model.

func_details.relevant_paper:
Energy Pointing Game (EPG) measures the concentration of attribution energy within the mask, the
fraction of positive attributions inside the bounding boxes:
$$\label{eq:epg}
    \text{EPG}_k = \frac{\sum_{h=1}^H\sum_{w=1}^W M_{k,hw} A^+_{k,hw}}{\sum_{h=1}^H\sum_{w=1}^W A^+_{k,hw}}\;.$$

In addition to
the losses described in prior work, we propose to also evaluate using
the score (, [\[eq:epg\]](#eq:epg){reference-type="ref"
reference="eq:epg"}) as a loss function for model guidance, as it is
fully differentiable. In particular, we simply define it as
$$\label{eq:energyloss}
\textstyle
    \mathcal{L}_{\text{loc},k} = -\text{EPG}_k.$$ Unlike existing
localization losses that either (i) do not constrain attributions across
the entire input (, ), or (ii) force the model to attribute uniformly
within the mask even if it includes irrelevant background regions (, ),
maximizing the score jointly optimizes for higher attribution energy
within the mask and lower attribution energy outside the mask. By not
enforcing a uniformity prior, we find that the loss is able to provide
effective guidance while allowing the model to learn freely what to
focus on within the bounding boxes

func_details.relevant_paper:
Energy Pointing Game (EPG) measures the concentration of attribution energy within the mask, the
fraction of positive attributions inside the bounding boxes:
$$\label{eq:epg}
    \text{EPG}_k = \frac{\sum_{h=1}^H\sum_{w=1}^W M_{k,hw} A^+_{k,hw}}{\sum_{h=1}^H\sum_{w=1}^W A^+_{k,hw}}\;.$$

In addition to
the losses described in prior work, we propose to also evaluate using
the score (, [\[eq:epg\]](#eq:epg){reference-type="ref"
reference="eq:epg"}) as a loss function for model guidance, as it is
fully differentiable. In particular, we simply define it as
$$\label{eq:energyloss}
\textstyle
    \mathcal{L}_{\text{loc},k} = -\text{EPG}_k.$$ Unlike existing
localization losses that either (i) do not constrain attributions across
the entire input (, ), or (ii) force the model to attribute uniformly
within the mask even if it includes irrelevant background regions (, ),
maximizing the score jointly optimizes for higher attribution energy
within the mask and lower attribution energy outside the mask. By not
enforcing a uniformity prior, we find that the loss is able to provide
effective guidance while allowing the model to learn freely what to
focus on within the bounding boxes

func_details.relevant_paper:
B-cos attributions are generated using the inherently-interpretable networks,
which promote alignment between the input $\mathbf x$ and a dynamic
weight matrix $\mathbf W(\mathbf x)$ during optimization. In our
experiments, we use the contribution maps given by the element-wise
product of the dynamic weights with the input
($\mathbf W^T_k(\mathbf x)\odot \mathbf x$), which faithfully represent
the contribution of each pixel to class $k$. To be able to guide models,
we developed a differentiable implementation of explanations, see
supplement.

func_details.relevant_paper:
Energy Pointing Game (EPG) measures the concentration of attribution energy within the mask, the
fraction of positive attributions inside the bounding boxes:
$$\label{eq:epg}
    \text{EPG}_k = \frac{\sum_{h=1}^H\sum_{w=1}^W M_{k,hw} A^+_{k,hw}}{\sum_{h=1}^H\sum_{w=1}^W A^+_{k,hw}}\;.$$

In addition to
the losses described in prior work, we propose to also evaluate using
the score (, [\[eq:epg\]](#eq:epg){reference-type="ref"
reference="eq:epg"}) as a loss function for model guidance, as it is
fully differentiable. In particular, we simply define it as
$$\label{eq:energyloss}
\textstyle
    \mathcal{L}_{\text{loc},k} = -\text{EPG}_k.$$ Unlike existing
localization losses that either (i) do not constrain attributions across
the entire input (, ), or (ii) force the model to attribute uniformly
within the mask even if it includes irrelevant background regions (, ),
maximizing the score jointly optimizes for higher attribution energy
within the mask and lower attribution energy outside the mask. By not
enforcing a uniformity prior, we find that the loss is able to provide
effective guidance while allowing the model to learn freely what to
focus on within the bounding boxes

func_details.relevant_paper:
GradCam computes importance attributions as a ReLU-thresholded,
gradient-weighted sum of activation maps. In detail, it is given by
$\text{ReLU}(\sum_c \alpha_c^k \odot U_c)$ with $c$ denoting the channel
dimension, and $\alpha^k$ the average-pooled gradients of the output for
class $k$ with respect to the activations $U$ of the last convolutional
layer in the model.

    def apply_post_processing(self, attributions):
        """

          - Binarization
          - Interpolation

func_details.relevant_paper:
Energy Pointing Game (EPG) measures the concentration of attribution energy within the mask, the
fraction of positive attributions inside the bounding boxes:
$$\label{eq:epg}
    \text{EPG}_k = \frac{\sum_{h=1}^H\sum_{w=1}^W M_{k,hw} A^+_{k,hw}}{\sum_{h=1}^H\sum_{w=1}^W A^+_{k,hw}}\;.$$

In addition to
the losses described in prior work, we propose to also evaluate using
the score (, [\[eq:epg\]](#eq:epg){reference-type="ref"
reference="eq:epg"}) as a loss function for model guidance, as it is
fully differentiable. In particular, we simply define it as
$$\label{eq:energyloss}
\textstyle
    \mathcal{L}_{\text{loc},k} = -\text{EPG}_k.$$ Unlike existing
localization losses that either (i) do not constrain attributions across
the entire input (, ), or (ii) force the model to attribute uniformly
within the mask even if it includes irrelevant background regions (, ),
maximizing the score jointly optimizes for higher attribution energy
within the mask and lower attribution energy outside the mask. By not
enforcing a uniformity prior, we find that the loss is able to provide
effective guidance while allowing the model to learn freely what to
focus on within the bounding boxes

func_details.relevant_paper:
B-cos attributions are generated using the inherently-interpretable networks,
which promote alignment between the input $\mathbf x$ and a dynamic
weight matrix $\mathbf W(\mathbf x)$ during optimization. In our
experiments, we use the contribution maps given by the element-wise
product of the dynamic weights with the input
($\mathbf W^T_k(\mathbf x)\odot \mathbf x$), which faithfully represent
the contribution of each pixel to class $k$. To be able to guide models,
we developed a differentiable implementation of explanations, see
supplement.

func_details.relevant_paper:
GradCam computes importance attributions as a ReLU-thresholded,
gradient-weighted sum of activation maps. In detail, it is given by
$\text{ReLU}(\sum_c \alpha_c^k \odot U_c)$ with $c$ denoting the channel
dimension, and $\alpha^k$ the average-pooled gradients of the output for
class $k$ with respect to the activations $U$ of the last convolutional
layer in the model.

func_details.relevant_paper:
Energy Pointing Game (EPG) measures the concentration of attribution energy within the mask, the
fraction of positive attributions inside the bounding boxes:
$$\label{eq:epg}
    \text{EPG}_k = \frac{\sum_{h=1}^H\sum_{w=1}^W M_{k,hw} A^+_{k,hw}}{\sum_{h=1}^H\sum_{w=1}^W A^+_{k,hw}}\;.$$

In addition to
the losses described in prior work, we propose to also evaluate using
the score (, [\[eq:epg\]](#eq:epg){reference-type="ref"
reference="eq:epg"}) as a loss function for model guidance, as it is
fully differentiable. In particular, we simply define it as
$$\label{eq:energyloss}
\textstyle
    \mathcal{L}_{\text{loc},k} = -\text{EPG}_k.$$ Unlike existing
localization losses that either (i) do not constrain attributions across
the entire input (, ), or (ii) force the model to attribute uniformly
within the mask even if it includes irrelevant background regions (, ),
maximizing the score jointly optimizes for higher attribution energy
within the mask and lower attribution energy outside the mask. By not
enforcing a uniformity prior, we find that the loss is able to provide
effective guidance while allowing the model to learn freely what to
focus on within the bounding boxes

func_details.relevant_paper:
B-cos attributions are generated using the inherently-interpretable networks,
which promote alignment between the input $\mathbf x$ and a dynamic
weight matrix $\mathbf W(\mathbf x)$ during optimization. In our
experiments, we use the contribution maps given by the element-wise
product of the dynamic weights with the input
($\mathbf W^T_k(\mathbf x)\odot \mathbf x$), which faithfully represent
the contribution of each pixel to class $k$. To be able to guide models,
we developed a differentiable implementation of explanations, see
supplement.

func_details.name: __call__
func_details.relevant_paper:
Energy Pointing Game (EPG) measures the concentration of attribution energy within the mask, the
fraction of positive attributions inside the bounding boxes:
$$\label{eq:epg}
    \text{EPG}_k = \frac{\sum_{h=1}^H\sum_{w=1}^W M_{k,hw} A^+_{k,hw}}{\sum_{h=1}^H\sum_{w=1}^W A^+_{k,hw}}\;.$$

In addition to
the losses described in prior work, we propose to also evaluate using
the score (, [\[eq:epg\]](#eq:epg){reference-type="ref"
reference="eq:epg"}) as a loss function for model guidance, as it is
fully differentiable. In particular, we simply define it as
$$\label{eq:energyloss}
\textstyle
    \mathcal{L}_{\text{loc},k} = -\text{EPG}_k.$$ Unlike existing
localization losses that either (i) do not constrain attributions across
the entire input (, ), or (ii) force the model to attribute uniformly
within the mask even if it includes irrelevant background regions (, ),
maximizing the score jointly optimizes for higher attribution energy
within the mask and lower attribution energy outside the mask. By not
enforcing a uniformity prior, we find that the loss is able to provide
effective guidance while allowing the model to learn freely what to
focus on within the bounding boxes

which promote alignment between the input $\mathbf x$ and a dynamic
weight matrix $\mathbf W(\mathbf x)$ during optimization. In our
experiments, we use the contribution maps given by the element-wise
product of the dynamic weights with the input
($\mathbf W^T_k(\mathbf x)\odot \mathbf x$), which faithfully represent
the contribution of each pixel to class $k$. To be able to guide models,
we developed a differentiable implementation of explanations, see
supplement.

func_details.relevant_paper:
Energy Pointing Game (EPG) measures the concentration of attribution energy within the mask, the
fraction of positive attributions inside the bounding boxes:
$$\label{eq:epg}
    \text{EPG}_k = \frac{\sum_{h=1}^H\sum_{w=1}^W M_{k,hw} A^+_{k,hw}}{\sum_{h=1}^H\sum_{w=1}^W A^+_{k,hw}}\;.$$

In addition to
the losses described in prior work, we propose to also evaluate using
the score (, [\[eq:epg\]](#eq:epg){reference-type="ref"
reference="eq:epg"}) as a loss function for model guidance, as it is
fully differentiable. In particular, we simply define it as
$$\label{eq:energyloss}
\textstyle
    \mathcal{L}_{\text{loc},k} = -\text{EPG}_k.$$ Unlike existing
localization losses that either (i) do not constrain attributions across
the entire input (, ), or (ii) force the model to attribute uniformly
within the mask even if it includes irrelevant background regions (, ),
maximizing the score jointly optimizes for higher attribution energy
within the mask and lower attribution energy outside the mask. By not
enforcing a uniformity prior, we find that the loss is able to provide
effective guidance while allowing the model to learn freely what to
focus on within the bounding boxes

func_details.relevant_paper:
Energy Pointing Game (EPG) measures the concentration of attribution energy within the mask, the
fraction of positive attributions inside the bounding boxes:
$$\label{eq:epg}
    \text{EPG}_k = \frac{\sum_{h=1}^H\sum_{w=1}^W M_{k,hw} A^+_{k,hw}}{\sum_{h=1}^H\sum_{w=1}^W A^+_{k,hw}}\;.$$

In addition to
the losses described in prior work, we propose to also evaluate using
the score (, [\[eq:epg\]](#eq:epg){reference-type="ref"
reference="eq:epg"}) as a loss function for model guidance, as it is
fully differentiable. In particular, we simply define it as
$$\label{eq:energyloss}
\textstyle
    \mathcal{L}_{\text{loc},k} = -\text{EPG}_k.$$ Unlike existing
localization losses that either (i) do not constrain attributions across
the entire input (, ), or (ii) force the model to attribute uniformly
within the mask even if it includes irrelevant background regions (, ),
maximizing the score jointly optimizes for higher attribution energy
within the mask and lower attribution energy outside the mask. By not
enforcing a uniformity prior, we find that the loss is able to provide
effective guidance while allowing the model to learn freely what to
focus on within the bounding boxes

func_details.relevant_paper:
B-cos attributions are generated using the inherently-interpretable networks,
which promote alignment between the input $\mathbf x$ and a dynamic
weight matrix $\mathbf W(\mathbf x)$ during optimization. In our
experiments, we use the contribution maps given by the element-wise
product of the dynamic weights with the input
($\mathbf W^T_k(\mathbf x)\odot \mathbf x$), which faithfully represent
the contribution of each pixel to class $k$. To be able to guide models,
we developed a differentiable implementation of explanations, see
supplement.

func_details.relevant_paper:
Energy Pointing Game (EPG) measures the concentration of attribution energy within the mask, the
fraction of positive attributions inside the bounding boxes:
$$\label{eq:epg}
    \text{EPG}_k = \frac{\sum_{h=1}^H\sum_{w=1}^W M_{k,hw} A^+_{k,hw}}{\sum_{h=1}^H\sum_{w=1}^W A^+_{k,hw}}\;.$$

In addition to
the losses described in prior work, we propose to also evaluate using
the score (, [\[eq:epg\]](#eq:epg){reference-type="ref"
reference="eq:epg"}) as a loss function for model guidance, as it is
fully differentiable. In particular, we simply define it as
$$\label{eq:energyloss}
\textstyle
    \mathcal{L}_{\text{loc},k} = -\text{EPG}_k.$$ Unlike existing
localization losses that either (i) do not constrain attributions across
the entire input (, ), or (ii) force the model to attribute uniformly
within the mask even if it includes irrelevant background regions (, ),
maximizing the score jointly optimizes for higher attribution energy
within the mask and lower attribution energy outside the mask. By not
enforcing a uniformity prior, we find that the loss is able to provide
effective guidance while allowing the model to learn freely what to
focus on within the bounding boxes

func_details.relevant_paper:
B-cos attributions are generated using the inherently-interpretable networks,
which promote alignment between the input $\mathbf x$ and a dynamic
weight matrix $\mathbf W(\mathbf x)$ during optimization. In our
experiments, we use the contribution maps given by the element-wise
product of the dynamic weights with the input
($\mathbf W^T_k(\mathbf x)\odot \mathbf x$), which faithfully represent
the contribution of each pixel to class $k$. To be able to guide models,
we developed a differentiable implementation of explanations, see
supplement.

func_details.relevant_paper:
Energy Pointing Game (EPG) measures the concentration of attribution energy within the mask, the
fraction of positive attributions inside the bounding boxes:
$$\label{eq:epg}
    \text{EPG}_k = \frac{\sum_{h=1}^H\sum_{w=1}^W M_{k,hw} A^+_{k,hw}}{\sum_{h=1}^H\sum_{w=1}^W A^+_{k,hw}}\;.$$

In addition to
the losses described in prior work, we propose to also evaluate using
the score (, [\[eq:epg\]](#eq:epg){reference-type="ref"
reference="eq:epg"}) as a loss function for model guidance, as it is
fully differentiable. In particular, we simply define it as
$$\label{eq:energyloss}
\textstyle
    \mathcal{L}_{\text{loc},k} = -\text{EPG}_k.$$ Unlike existing
localization losses that either (i) do not constrain attributions across
the entire input (, ), or (ii) force the model to attribute uniformly
within the mask even if it includes irrelevant background regions (, ),
maximizing the score jointly optimizes for higher attribution energy
within the mask and lower attribution energy outside the mask. By not
enforcing a uniformity prior, we find that the loss is able to provide
effective guidance while allowing the model to learn freely what to
focus on within the bounding boxes

func_details.relevant_paper:
Energy Pointing Game (EPG) measures the concentration of attribution energy within the mask, the
fraction of positive attributions inside the bounding boxes:
$$\label{eq:epg}
    \text{EPG}_k = \frac{\sum_{h=1}^H\sum_{w=1}^W M_{k,hw} A^+_{k,hw}}{\sum_{h=1}^H\sum_{w=1}^W A^+_{k,hw}}\;.$$

In addition to
the losses described in prior work, we propose to also evaluate using
the score (, [\[eq:epg\]](#eq:epg){reference-type="ref"
reference="eq:epg"}) as a loss function for model guidance, as it is
fully differentiable. In particular, we simply define it as
$$\label{eq:energyloss}
\textstyle
    \mathcal{L}_{\text{loc},k} = -\text{EPG}_k.$$ Unlike existing
localization losses that either (i) do not constrain attributions across
the entire input (, ), or (ii) force the model to attribute uniformly
within the mask even if it includes irrelevant background regions (, ),
maximizing the score jointly optimizes for higher attribution energy
within the mask and lower attribution energy outside the mask. By not
enforcing a uniformity prior, we find that the loss is able to provide
effective guidance while allowing the model to learn freely what to
focus on within the bounding boxes

dimension, and $\alpha^k$ the average-pooled gradients of the output for
class $k$ with respect to the activations $U$ of the last convolutional
layer in the model.

func_details.relevant_paper:
RRR* introduced the RRR loss to regularize the normalized input gradients
$\hat{A}_{k,hw}$ as $$\label{eq:rrr}
    \textstyle \mathcal{L}_{\text{loc},k} = \sum_{h=1}^H\sum_{w=1}^W (1-M_{k,hw}) \hat{A}_{k,hw}^2 \;.$$
To extend it to our setting, we take $\hat{A}_{k,hw}$ to be given by an
arbitrary attribution method (); we denote this generalized version by RRR*.
In contrast to the loss, only regularizes attributions *outside* the
ground truth masks. While it thus does not introduce a uniformity prior
similar to the loss, it also does not explicitly promote high importance
attributions inside the masks.

func_details.relevant_paper:
Per-pixel cross entropy loss (PPCE) applies a binary cross entropy loss between the mask and the normalized
positive annotations $\hat A_{k}^+$, thus guiding the model to maximize
the attributions inside the mask: $$\label{eq:ppce}
\textstyle
    \mathcal{L}_{\text{loc},k} = -\frac{1}{\lVert M_k \rVert_1}\sum_{h=1}^H\sum_{w=1}^W M_{k,hw}\log(\hat{A}_{k,hw}^+) \;.$$
As PPCE does not constrain attributions outside the mask, there is no
explicit pressure to avoid spurious features.

---- gradient_to_image (from bcos/models/bcos_common.py) ----
    def gradient_to_image(
        cls,
        image: "Tensor",
        linear_mapping: "Tensor",
        smooth: int = 0,
        alpha_percentile: float = 99.5,
    ) -> "np.ndarray":
        # shape of img and linmap is [C, H, W], summing over first dimension gives the contribution map per location
        contribs = (image * linear_mapping).sum(0, keepdim=True)
        contribs = contribs[0]
        # Normalise each pixel vector (r, g, b, 1-r, 1-g, 1-b) s.t. max entry is 1, maintaining direction
        rgb_grad = linear_mapping / (
            linear_mapping.abs().max(0, keepdim=True)[0] + 1e-12
        )
        # clip off values below 0 (i.e., set negatively weighted channels to 0 weighting)
        rgb_grad = rgb_grad.clamp(0)
        # normalise s.t. each pair (e.g., r and 1-r) sums to 1 and only use resulting rgb values
        rgb_grad = cls._to_numpy(rgb_grad[:3] / (rgb_grad[:3] + rgb_grad[3:] + 1e-12))

        # Set alpha value to the strength (L2 norm) of each location's gradient
        alpha = linear_mapping.norm(p=2, dim=0, keepdim=True)
        # Only show positive contributions
        alpha = torch.where(contribs[None] < 0, torch.zeros_like(alpha) + 1e-12, alpha)
        if smooth:
            alpha = F.avg_pool2d(alpha, smooth, stride=1, padding=(smooth - 1) // 2)
        alpha = cls._to_numpy(alpha)
        alpha = (alpha / np.percentile(alpha, alpha_percentile)).clip(0, 1)

        rgb_grad = np.concatenate([rgb_grad, alpha], axis=0)
        # Reshaping to [H, W, C]
        grad_image = rgb_grad.transpose((1, 2, 0))
        return grad_image

func_details.name: __call__
func_details.relevant_paper:
RRR* introduced the RRR loss to regularize the normalized input gradients
$\hat{A}_{k,hw}$ as $$\label{eq:rrr}
    \textstyle \mathcal{L}_{\text{loc},k} = \sum_{h=1}^H\sum_{w=1}^W (1-M_{k,hw}) \hat{A}_{k,hw}^2 \;.$$
To extend it to our setting, we take $\hat{A}_{k,hw}$ to be given by an
arbitrary attribution method (); we denote this generalized version by RRR*.
In contrast to the loss, only regularizes attributions *outside* the
ground truth masks. While it thus does not introduce a uniformity prior
similar to the loss, it also does not explicitly promote high importance
attributions inside the masks.

func_details.relevant_paper:
Per-pixel cross entropy loss (PPCE) applies a binary cross entropy loss between the mask and the normalized
positive annotations $\hat A_{k}^+$, thus guiding the model to maximize
the attributions inside the mask: $$\label{eq:ppce}
\textstyle
    \mathcal{L}_{\text{loc},k} = -\frac{1}{\lVert M_k \rVert_1}\sum_{h=1}^H\sum_{w=1}^W M_{k,hw}\log(\hat{A}_{k,hw}^+) \;.$$
As PPCE does not constrain attributions outside the mask, there is no
explicit pressure to avoid spurious features.

---- gradient_to_image (from bcos/models/bcos_common.py) ----
    def gradient_to_image(
        cls,
        image: "Tensor",
        linear_mapping: "Tensor",
        smooth: int = 0,
        alpha_percentile: float = 99.5,
    ) -> "np.ndarray":
        # shape of img and linmap is [C, H, W], summing over first dimension gives the contribution map per location
        contribs = (image * linear_mapping).sum(0, keepdim=True)
        contribs = contribs[0]
        # Normalise each pixel vector (r, g, b, 1-r, 1-g, 1-b) s.t. max entry is 1, maintaining direction
        rgb_grad = linear_mapping / (
            linear_mapping.abs().max(0, keepdim=True)[0] + 1e-12
        )
        # clip off values below 0 (i.e., set negatively weighted channels to 0 weighting)
        rgb_grad = rgb_grad.clamp(0)
        # normalise s.t. each pair (e.g., r and 1-r) sums to 1 and only use resulting rgb values
        rgb_grad = cls._to_numpy(rgb_grad[:3] / (rgb_grad[:3] + rgb_grad[3:] + 1e-12))

        # Set alpha value to the strength (L2 norm) of each location's gradient
        alpha = linear_mapping.norm(p=2, dim=0, keepdim=True)
        # Only show positive contributions
        alpha = torch.where(contribs[None] < 0, torch.zeros_like(alpha) + 1e-12, alpha)
        if smooth:
            alpha = F.avg_pool2d(alpha, smooth, stride=1, padding=(smooth - 1) // 2)
        alpha = cls._to_numpy(alpha)
        alpha = (alpha / np.percentile(alpha, alpha_percentile)).clip(0, 1)

        rgb_grad = np.concatenate([rgb_grad, alpha], axis=0)
        # Reshaping to [H, W, C]
        grad_image = rgb_grad.transpose((1, 2, 0))
        return grad_image

    def gradient_to_image(
        cls,
        image: "Tensor",
        linear_mapping: "Tensor",
        smooth: int = 0,
        alpha_percentile: float = 99.5,
    ) -> "np.ndarray":
        # shape of img and linmap is [C, H, W], summing over first dimension gives the contribution map per location
        contribs = (image * linear_mapping).sum(0, keepdim=True)
        contribs = contribs[0]
        # Normalise each pixel vector (r, g, b, 1-r, 1-g, 1-b) s.t. max entry is 1, maintaining direction
        rgb_grad = linear_mapping / (
            linear_mapping.abs().max(0, keepdim=True)[0] + 1e-12
        )
        # clip off values below 0 (i.e., set negatively weighted channels to 0 weighting)
        rgb_grad = rgb_grad.clamp(0)
        # normalise s.t. each pair (e.g., r and 1-r) sums to 1 and only use resulting rgb values
        rgb_grad = cls._to_numpy(rgb_grad[:3] / (rgb_grad[:3] + rgb_grad[3:] + 1e-12))

        # Set alpha value to the strength (L2 norm) of each location's gradient
        alpha = linear_mapping.norm(p=2, dim=0, keepdim=True)
        # Only show positive contributions
        alpha = torch.where(contribs[None] < 0, torch.zeros_like(alpha) + 1e-12, alpha)
        if smooth:
            alpha = F.avg_pool2d(alpha, smooth, stride=1, padding=(smooth - 1) // 2)
        alpha = cls._to_numpy(alpha)
        alpha = (alpha / np.percentile(alpha, alpha_percentile)).clip(0, 1)

        rgb_grad = np.concatenate([rgb_grad, alpha], axis=0)
        # Reshaping to [H, W, C]
        grad_image = rgb_grad.transpose((1, 2, 0))
        return grad_image

    def explanation_mode(self):
        """
        Creates a context manager which puts model in to explanation
        mode and when exiting puts it into normal mode back again.
        """
        return self._expl_mode_ctx



---- gradient_to_image (from bcos/models/bcos_common.py) ----
    def gradient_to_image(
        cls,
        image: "Tensor",
        linear_mapping: "Tensor",
        smooth: int = 0,
        alpha_percentile: float = 99.5,
    ) -> "np.ndarray":
        # shape of img and linmap is [C, H, W], summing over first dimension gives the contribution map per location
        contribs = (image * linear_mapping).sum(0, keepdim=True)
        contribs = contribs[0]
        # Normalise each pixel vector (r, g, b, 1-r, 1-g, 1-b) s.t. max entry is 1, maintaining direction
        rgb_grad = linear_mapping / (
            linear_mapping.abs().max(0, keepdim=True)[0] + 1e-12
        )
        # clip off values below 0 (i.e., set negatively weighted channels to 0 weighting)
        rgb_grad = rgb_grad.clamp(0)
        # normalise s.t. each pair (e.g., r and 1-r) sums to 1 and only use resulting rgb values
        rgb_grad = cls._to_numpy(rgb_grad[:3] / (rgb_grad[:3] + rgb_grad[3:] + 1e-12))

        # Set alpha value to the strength (L2 norm) of each location's gradient
        alpha = linear_mapping.norm(p=2, dim=0, keepdim=True)
        # Only show positive contributions
        alpha = torch.where(contribs[None] < 0, torch.zeros_like(alpha) + 1e-12, alpha)
        if smooth:
            alpha = F.avg_pool2d(alpha, smooth, stride=1, padding=(smooth - 1) // 2)
        alpha = cls._to_numpy(alpha)
        alpha = (alpha / np.percentile(alpha, alpha_percentile)).clip(0, 1)

        rgb_grad = np.concatenate([rgb_grad, alpha], axis=0)
        # Reshaping to [H, W, C]
        grad_image = rgb_grad.transpose((1, 2, 0))
        return grad_image

weight matrix $\mathbf W(\mathbf x)$ during optimization. In our
experiments, we use the contribution maps given by the element-wise

func_details.relevant_paper:
RRR* introduced the RRR loss to regularize the normalized input gradients
$\hat{A}_{k,hw}$ as $$\label{eq:rrr}
    \textstyle \mathcal{L}_{\text{loc},k} = \sum_{h=1}^H\sum_{w=1}^W (1-M_{k,hw}) \hat{A}_{k,hw}^2 \;.$$
To extend it to our setting, we take $\hat{A}_{k,hw}$ to be given by an
arbitrary attribution method (); we denote this generalized version by RRR*.
In contrast to the loss, only regularizes attributions *outside* the
ground truth masks. While it thus does not introduce a uniformity prior
similar to the loss, it also does not explicitly promote high importance
attributions inside the masks.

func_details.relevant_paper:
Per-pixel cross entropy loss (PPCE) applies a binary cross entropy loss between the mask and the normalized
positive annotations $\hat A_{k}^+$, thus guiding the model to maximize
the attributions inside the mask: $$\label{eq:ppce}
\textstyle
    \mathcal{L}_{\text{loc},k} = -\frac{1}{\lVert M_k \rVert_1}\sum_{h=1}^H\sum_{w=1}^W M_{k,hw}\log(\hat{A}_{k,hw}^+) \;.$$
As PPCE does not constrain attributions outside the mask, there is no
explicit pressure to avoid spurious features.

---- gradient_to_image (from bcos/models/bcos_common.py) ----
    def gradient_to_image(
        cls,
        image: "Tensor",
        linear_mapping: "Tensor",
        smooth: int = 0,
        alpha_percentile: float = 99.5,
    ) -> "np.ndarray":
        # shape of img and linmap is [C, H, W], summing over first dimension gives the contribution map per location
        contribs = (image * linear_mapping).sum(0, keepdim=True)
        contribs = contribs[0]
        # Normalise each pixel vector (r, g, b, 1-r, 1-g, 1-b) s.t. max entry is 1, maintaining direction
        rgb_grad = linear_mapping / (
            linear_mapping.abs().max(0, keepdim=True)[0] + 1e-12
        )
        # clip off values below 0 (i.e., set negatively weighted channels to 0 weighting)
        rgb_grad = rgb_grad.clamp(0)
        # normalise s.t. each pair (e.g., r and 1-r) sums to 1 and only use resulting rgb values
        rgb_grad = cls._to_numpy(rgb_grad[:3] / (rgb_grad[:3] + rgb_grad[3:] + 1e-12))

        # Set alpha value to the strength (L2 norm) of each location's gradient
        alpha = linear_mapping.norm(p=2, dim=0, keepdim=True)
        # Only show positive contributions
        alpha = torch.where(contribs[None] < 0, torch.zeros_like(alpha) + 1e-12, alpha)
        if smooth:
            alpha = F.avg_pool2d(alpha, smooth, stride=1, padding=(smooth - 1) // 2)
        alpha = cls._to_numpy(alpha)
        alpha = (alpha / np.percentile(alpha, alpha_percentile)).clip(0, 1)

        rgb_grad = np.concatenate([rgb_grad, alpha], axis=0)
        # Reshaping to [H, W, C]
        grad_image = rgb_grad.transpose((1, 2, 0))
        return grad_image

    def apply_post_processing(self, attributions):
        """

          - Keeping only positive values
          - Binarization
          - Interpolation

        attributions = self.check_only_positive(attributions)

func_details.relevant_paper:
GradCam computes importance attributions as a ReLU-thresholded,
gradient-weighted sum of activation maps. In detail, it is given by
$\text{ReLU}(\sum_c \alpha_c^k \odot U_c)$ with $c$ denoting the channel
dimension, and $\alpha^k$ the average-pooled gradients of the output for
class $k$ with respect to the activations $U$ of the last convolutional
layer in the model.

func_details.relevant_paper:
RRR* introduced the RRR loss to regularize the normalized input gradients
$\hat{A}_{k,hw}$ as $$\label{eq:rrr}
    \textstyle \mathcal{L}_{\text{loc},k} = \sum_{h=1}^H\sum_{w=1}^W (1-M_{k,hw}) \hat{A}_{k,hw}^2 \;.$$
To extend it to our setting, we take $\hat{A}_{k,hw}$ to be given by an
arbitrary attribution method (); we denote this generalized version by RRR*.
In contrast to the loss, only regularizes attributions *outside* the
ground truth masks. While it thus does not introduce a uniformity prior
similar to the loss, it also does not explicitly promote high importance
attributions inside the masks.

func_details.name: __call__
func_details.relevant_paper:
Per-pixel cross entropy loss (PPCE) applies a binary cross entropy loss between the mask and the normalized
positive annotations $\hat A_{k}^+$, thus guiding the model to maximize
the attributions inside the mask: $$\label{eq:ppce}
\textstyle
    \mathcal{L}_{\text{loc},k} = -\frac{1}{\lVert M_k \rVert_1}\sum_{h=1}^H\sum_{w=1}^W M_{k,hw}\log(\hat{A}_{k,hw}^+) \;.$$
As PPCE does not constrain attributions outside the mask, there is no
explicit pressure to avoid spurious features.

func_details.relevant_paper:
GradCam computes importance attributions as a ReLU-thresholded,
gradient-weighted sum of activation maps. In detail, it is given by
$\text{ReLU}(\sum_c \alpha_c^k \odot U_c)$ with $c$ denoting the channel
dimension, and $\alpha^k$ the average-pooled gradients of the output for
class $k$ with respect to the activations $U$ of the last convolutional
layer in the model.

func_details.relevant_paper:
B-cos attributions are generated using the inherently-interpretable networks,
which promote alignment between the input $\mathbf x$ and a dynamic
weight matrix $\mathbf W(\mathbf x)$ during optimization. In our
experiments, we use the contribution maps given by the element-wise
product of the dynamic weights with the input
($\mathbf W^T_k(\mathbf x)\odot \mathbf x$), which faithfully represent
the contribution of each pixel to class $k$. To be able to guide models,
we developed a differentiable implementation of explanations, see
supplement.

    def apply_post_processing(self, attributions):
        """
        Applies post-processing steps to attributions
        
        Post processing steps:
          - Keeping only positive values
          - Binarization
          - Interpolation

        Args:
        attributions (tensor): Computed attributions

        Returns:
        tensor: Post-processed attributions
        """
        attributions = self.check_only_positive(attributions)
        attributions = self.check_binarize(attributions)
        attributions = self.check_interpolate(attributions)
        return attributions

func_details.relevant_paper:
RRR* introduced the RRR loss to regularize the normalized input gradients
$\hat{A}_{k,hw}$ as $$\label{eq:rrr}
    \textstyle \mathcal{L}_{\text{loc},k} = \sum_{h=1}^H\sum_{w=1}^W (1-M_{k,hw}) \hat{A}_{k,hw}^2 \;.$$
To extend it to our setting, we take $\hat{A}_{k,hw}$ to be given by an
arbitrary attribution method (); we denote this generalized version by RRR*.
In contrast to the loss, only regularizes attributions *outside* the
ground truth masks. While it thus does not introduce a uniformity prior
similar to the loss, it also does not explicitly promote high importance
attributions inside the masks.

func_details.relevant_paper:
Per-pixel cross entropy loss (PPCE) applies a binary cross entropy loss between the mask and the normalized
positive annotations $\hat A_{k}^+$, thus guiding the model to maximize
the attributions inside the mask: $$\label{eq:ppce}
\textstyle
    \mathcal{L}_{\text{loc},k} = -\frac{1}{\lVert M_k \rVert_1}\sum_{h=1}^H\sum_{w=1}^W M_{k,hw}\log(\hat{A}_{k,hw}^+) \;.$$

explicit pressure to avoid spurious features.

func_details.relevant_paper:
B-cos attributions are generated using the inherently-interpretable networks,
which promote alignment between the input $\mathbf x$ and a dynamic
weight matrix $\mathbf W(\mathbf x)$ during optimization. In our
experiments, we use the contribution maps given by the element-wise
product of the dynamic weights with the input
($\mathbf W^T_k(\mathbf x)\odot \mathbf x$), which faithfully represent
the contribution of each pixel to class $k$. To be able to guide models,
we developed a differentiable implementation of explanations, see
supplement.

func_details.name: _call_single
func_details.relevant_paper:
B-cos attributions are generated using the inherently-interpretable networks,
which promote alignment between the input $\mathbf x$ and a dynamic
weight matrix $\mathbf W(\mathbf x)$ during optimization. In our
experiments, we use the contribution maps given by the element-wise
product of the dynamic weights with the input
($\mathbf W^T_k(\mathbf x)\odot \mathbf x$), which faithfully represent
the contribution of each pixel to class $k$. To be able to guide models,
we developed a differentiable implementation of explanations, see
supplement.

func_details.relevant_paper:
RRR* introduced the RRR loss to regularize the normalized input gradients
$\hat{A}_{k,hw}$ as $$\label{eq:rrr}
    \textstyle \mathcal{L}_{\text{loc},k} = \sum_{h=1}^H\sum_{w=1}^W (1-M_{k,hw}) \hat{A}_{k,hw}^2 \;.$$
To extend it to our setting, we take $\hat{A}_{k,hw}$ to be given by an
arbitrary attribution method (); we denote this generalized version by RRR*.
In contrast to the loss, only regularizes attributions *outside* the
ground truth masks. While it thus does not introduce a uniformity prior
similar to the loss, it also does not explicitly promote high importance
attributions inside the masks.

explicit pressure to avoid spurious features.

func_details.relevant_paper:
RRR* introduced the RRR loss to regularize the normalized input gradients
$\hat{A}_{k,hw}$ as $$\label{eq:rrr}
    \textstyle \mathcal{L}_{\text{loc},k} = \sum_{h=1}^H\sum_{w=1}^W (1-M_{k,hw}) \hat{A}_{k,hw}^2 \;.$$
To extend it to our setting, we take $\hat{A}_{k,hw}$ to be given by an
arbitrary attribution method (); we denote this generalized version by RRR*.
In contrast to the loss, only regularizes attributions *outside* the
ground truth masks. While it thus does not introduce a uniformity prior
similar to the loss, it also does not explicitly promote high importance
attributions inside the masks.

func_details.name: __call__
func_details.relevant_paper:
Per-pixel cross entropy loss (PPCE) applies a binary cross entropy loss between the mask and the normalized
positive annotations $\hat A_{k}^+$, thus guiding the model to maximize
the attributions inside the mask: $$\label{eq:ppce}
\textstyle
    \mathcal{L}_{\text{loc},k} = -\frac{1}{\lVert M_k \rVert_1}\sum_{h=1}^H\sum_{w=1}^W M_{k,hw}\log(\hat{A}_{k,hw}^+) \;.$$
As PPCE does not constrain attributions outside the mask, there is no
explicit pressure to avoid spurious features.

    def apply_post_processing(self, attributions):
        """

func_details.relevant_paper:
RRR* introduced the RRR loss to regularize the normalized input gradients
$\hat{A}_{k,hw}$ as $$\label{eq:rrr}
    \textstyle \mathcal{L}_{\text{loc},k} = \sum_{h=1}^H\sum_{w=1}^W (1-M_{k,hw}) \hat{A}_{k,hw}^2 \;.$$
To extend it to our setting, we take $\hat{A}_{k,hw}$ to be given by an
arbitrary attribution method (); we denote this generalized version by RRR*.
In contrast to the loss, only regularizes attributions *outside* the
ground truth masks. While it thus does not introduce a uniformity prior
similar to the loss, it also does not explicitly promote high importance
attributions inside the masks.

positive annotations $\hat A_{k}^+$, thus guiding the model to maximize
the attributions inside the mask: $$\label{eq:ppce}

explicit pressure to avoid spurious features.

which promote alignment between the input $\mathbf x$ and a dynamic
weight matrix $\mathbf W(\mathbf x)$ during optimization. In our
experiments, we use the contribution maps given by the element-wise
product of the dynamic weights with the input
($\mathbf W^T_k(\mathbf x)\odot \mathbf x$), which faithfully represent
the contribution of each pixel to class $k$. To be able to guide models,
we developed a differentiable implementation of explanations, see
supplement.

gradient-weighted sum of activation maps. In detail, it is given by

dimension, and $\alpha^k$ the average-pooled gradients of the output for
class $k$ with respect to the activations $U$ of the last convolutional
layer in the model.

RRR* introduced the RRR loss to regularize the normalized input gradients
$\hat{A}_{k,hw}$ as $$\label{eq:rrr}
    \textstyle \mathcal{L}_{\text{loc},k} = \sum_{h=1}^H\sum_{w=1}^W (1-M_{k,hw}) \hat{A}_{k,hw}^2 \;.$$
To extend it to our setting, we take $\hat{A}_{k,hw}$ to be given by an
arbitrary attribution method (); we denote this generalized version by RRR*.
In contrast to the loss, only regularizes attributions *outside* the
ground truth masks. While it thus does not introduce a uniformity prior
similar to the loss, it also does not explicitly promote high importance
attributions inside the masks.

:param bb_coordinates: A tensor 

:return: A scalar tensor

func_details.name: __call__
func_details.relevant_paper:
Per-pixel cross entropy loss (PPCE) applies a binary cross entropy loss between the mask and the normalized
positive annotations $\hat A_{k}^+$, thus guiding the model to maximize
the attributions inside the mask: $$\label{eq:ppce}
\textstyle
    \mathcal{L}_{\text{loc},k} = -\frac{1}{\lVert M_k \rVert_1}\sum_{h=1}^H\sum_{w=1}^W M_{k,hw}\log(\hat{A}_{k,hw}^+) \;.$$
As PPCE does not constrain attributions outside the mask, there is no
explicit pressure to avoid spurious features.
func_details.description:
Calculates the PPCE localization loss given the attributions and bounding box coordinates. 

:param attributions: A tensor 
:param bb_coordinates: A tensor 

:return: tensor

func_details.name: _call_batch_mode
func_details.relevant_paper:
B-cos attributions are generated using the inherently-interpretable networks,
which promote alignment between the input $\mathbf x$ and a dynamic
weight matrix $\mathbf W(\mathbf x)$ during optimization. In our
experiments, we use the contribution maps given by the element-wise
product of the dynamic weights with the input
($\mathbf W^T_k(\mathbf x)\odot \mathbf x$), which faithfully represent
the contribution of each pixel to class $k$. To be able to guide models,
we developed a differentiable implementation of explanations, see
supplement.
func_details.description:
Computes attributions of model outputs with respect to input features and applies post-processing.

:param output: A tensor 
:param classes: A tensor 
:param feature: A tensor 
:return: A tensor
func_details.code_context:
---- apply_post_processing (from attribution_methods.py) ----
    def apply_post_processing(self, attributions):
        """
        Applies post-processing steps to attributions
        
        Post processing steps:
          - Keeping only positive values
          - Binarization
          - Interpolation

        Args:
        attributions (tensor): Computed attributions

        Returns:
        tensor: Post-processed attributions
        """
        attributions = self.check_only_positive(attributions)
        attributions = self.check_binarize(attributions)
        attributions = self.check_interpolate(attributions)
        return attributions

func_details.name: _call_single
func_details.relevant_paper:
GradCam computes importance attributions as a ReLU-thresholded,
gradient-weighted sum of activation maps. In detail, it is given by
$\text{ReLU}(\sum_c \alpha_c^k \odot U_c)$ with $c$ denoting the channel
dimension, and $\alpha^k$ the average-pooled gradients of the output for
class $k$ with respect to the activations $U$ of the last convolutional
layer in the model.

:return: tensor

func_details.relevant_paper:
RRR* introduced the RRR loss to regularize the normalized input gradients
$\hat{A}_{k,hw}$ as $$\label{eq:rrr}
    \textstyle \mathcal{L}_{\text{loc},k} = \sum_{h=1}^H\sum_{w=1}^W (1-M_{k,hw}) \hat{A}_{k,hw}^2 \;.$$
To extend it to our setting, we take $\hat{A}_{k,hw}$ to be given by an
arbitrary attribution method (); we denote this generalized version by RRR*.
In contrast to the loss, only regularizes attributions *outside* the
ground truth masks. While it thus does not introduce a uniformity prior
similar to the loss, it also does not explicitly promote high importance
attributions inside the masks.

func_details.relevant_paper:
Per-pixel cross entropy loss (PPCE) applies a binary cross entropy loss between the mask and the normalized
positive annotations $\hat A_{k}^+$, thus guiding the model to maximize
the attributions inside the mask: $$\label{eq:ppce}
\textstyle
    \mathcal{L}_{\text{loc},k} = -\frac{1}{\lVert M_k \rVert_1}\sum_{h=1}^H\sum_{w=1}^W M_{k,hw}\log(\hat{A}_{k,hw}^+) \;.$$
As PPCE does not constrain attributions outside the mask, there is no
explicit pressure to avoid spurious features.

func_details.relevant_paper:
RRR* introduced the RRR loss to regularize the normalized input gradients
$\hat{A}_{k,hw}$ as $$\label{eq:rrr}
    \textstyle \mathcal{L}_{\text{loc},k} = \sum_{h=1}^H\sum_{w=1}^W (1-M_{k,hw}) \hat{A}_{k,hw}^2 \;.$$
To extend it to our setting, we take $\hat{A}_{k,hw}$ to be given by an
arbitrary attribution method (); we denote this generalized version by RRR*.
In contrast to the loss, only regularizes attributions *outside* the
ground truth masks. While it thus does not introduce a uniformity prior
similar to the loss, it also does not explicitly promote high importance
attributions inside the masks.

positive annotations $\hat A_{k}^+$, thus guiding the model to maximize
the attributions inside the mask: $$\label{eq:ppce}

explicit pressure to avoid spurious features.

func_details.relevant_paper:
RRR* introduced the RRR loss to regularize the normalized input gradients
$\hat{A}_{k,hw}$ as $$\label{eq:rrr}
    \textstyle \mathcal{L}_{\text{loc},k} = \sum_{h=1}^H\sum_{w=1}^W (1-M_{k,hw}) \hat{A}_{k,hw}^2 \;.$$
To extend it to our setting, we take $\hat{A}_{k,hw}$ to be given by an
arbitrary attribution method (); we denote this generalized version by RRR*.
In contrast to the loss, only regularizes attributions *outside* the
ground truth masks. While it thus does not introduce a uniformity prior
similar to the loss, it also does not explicitly promote high importance
attributions inside the masks.

        Creates a context manager which puts model in to explanation

---- gradient_to_image (from bcos/models/bcos_common.py) ----
    def gradient_to_image(
        cls,
        image: "Tensor",
        linear_mapping: "Tensor",
        smooth: int = 0,
        alpha_percentile: float = 99.5,
    ) -> "np.ndarray":
        # shape of img and linmap is [C, H, W], summing over first dimension gives the contribution map per location
        contribs = (image * linear_mapping).sum(0, keepdim=True)
        contribs = contribs[0]
        # Normalise each pixel vector (r, g, b, 1-r, 1-g, 1-b) s.t. max entry is 1, maintaining direction
        rgb_grad = linear_mapping / (
            linear_mapping.abs().max(0, keepdim=True)[0] + 1e-12
        )
        # clip off values below 0 (i.e., set negatively weighted channels to 0 weighting)
        rgb_grad = rgb_grad.clamp(0)
        # normalise s.t. each pair (e.g., r and 1-r) sums to 1 and only use resulting rgb values
        rgb_grad = cls._to_numpy(rgb_grad[:3] / (rgb_grad[:3] + rgb_grad[3:] + 1e-12))

        # Set alpha value to the strength (L2 norm) of each location's gradient
        alpha = linear_mapping.norm(p=2, dim=0, keepdim=True)
        # Only show positive contributions
        alpha = torch.where(contribs[None] < 0, torch.zeros_like(alpha) + 1e-12, alpha)
        if smooth:
            alpha = F.avg_pool2d(alpha, smooth, stride=1, padding=(smooth - 1) // 2)
        alpha = cls._to_numpy(alpha)
        alpha = (alpha / np.percentile(alpha, alpha_percentile)).clip(0, 1)

        rgb_grad = np.concatenate([rgb_grad, alpha], axis=0)
        # Reshaping to [H, W, C]
        grad_image = rgb_grad.transpose((1, 2, 0))
        return grad_image

RRR* introduced the RRR loss to regularize the normalized input gradients
$\hat{A}_{k,hw}$ as $$\label{eq:rrr}
    \textstyle \mathcal{L}_{\text{loc},k} = \sum_{h=1}^H\sum_{w=1}^W (1-M_{k,hw}) \hat{A}_{k,hw}^2 \;.$$
To extend it to our setting, we take $\hat{A}_{k,hw}$ to be given by an
arbitrary attribution method (); we denote this generalized version by RRR*.
In contrast to the loss, only regularizes attributions *outside* the
ground truth masks. While it thus does not introduce a uniformity prior
similar to the loss, it also does not explicitly promote high importance
attributions inside the masks.

---- gradient_to_image (from bcos/models/bcos_common.py) ----
    def gradient_to_image(
        cls,
        image: "Tensor",
        linear_mapping: "Tensor",
        smooth: int = 0,
        alpha_percentile: float = 99.5,
    ) -> "np.ndarray":
        # shape of img and linmap is [C, H, W], summing over first dimension gives the contribution map per location
        contribs = (image * linear_mapping).sum(0, keepdim=True)
        contribs = contribs[0]
        # Normalise each pixel vector (r, g, b, 1-r, 1-g, 1-b) s.t. max entry is 1, maintaining direction
        rgb_grad = linear_mapping / (
            linear_mapping.abs().max(0, keepdim=True)[0] + 1e-12
        )
        # clip off values below 0 (i.e., set negatively weighted channels to 0 weighting)
        rgb_grad = rgb_grad.clamp(0)
        # normalise s.t. each pair (e.g., r and 1-r) sums to 1 and only use resulting rgb values
        rgb_grad = cls._to_numpy(rgb_grad[:3] / (rgb_grad[:3] + rgb_grad[3:] + 1e-12))

        # Set alpha value to the strength (L2 norm) of each location's gradient
        alpha = linear_mapping.norm(p=2, dim=0, keepdim=True)
        # Only show positive contributions
        alpha = torch.where(contribs[None] < 0, torch.zeros_like(alpha) + 1e-12, alpha)
        if smooth:
            alpha = F.avg_pool2d(alpha, smooth, stride=1, padding=(smooth - 1) // 2)
        alpha = cls._to_numpy(alpha)
        alpha = (alpha / np.percentile(alpha, alpha_percentile)).clip(0, 1)

        rgb_grad = np.concatenate([rgb_grad, alpha], axis=0)
        # Reshaping to [H, W, C]
        grad_image = rgb_grad.transpose((1, 2, 0))
        return grad_image

weight matrix $\mathbf W(\mathbf x)$ during optimization. In our

    def apply_post_processing(self, attributions):
        """
        Applies post-processing steps to attributions
        
        Post processing steps:
          - Keeping only positive values
          - Binarization
          - Interpolation

        Args:
        attributions (tensor): Computed attributions

        Returns:
        tensor: Post-processed attributions
        """
        attributions = self.check_only_positive(attributions)

weight matrix $\mathbf W(\mathbf x)$ during optimization. In our
experiments, we use the contribution maps given by the element-wise
product of the dynamic weights with the input

the contribution of each pixel to class $k$. To be able to guide models,

    def apply_post_processing(self, attributions):
        """
        Applies post-processing steps to attributions
        
        Post processing steps:
          - Keeping only positive values
          - Binarization
          - Interpolation

        Args:
        attributions (tensor): Computed attributions

        Returns:
        tensor: Post-processed attributions
        """
        attributions = self.check_only_positive(attributions)
        attributions = self.check_binarize(attributions)
        attributions = self.check_interpolate(attributions)
        return attributions

func_details.name: __call__
func_details.relevant_paper:
RRR* introduced the RRR loss to regularize the normalized input gradients
$\hat{A}_{k,hw}$ as $$\label{eq:rrr}
    \textstyle \mathcal{L}_{\text{loc},k} = \sum_{h=1}^H\sum_{w=1}^W (1-M_{k,hw}) \hat{A}_{k,hw}^2 \;.$$
To extend it to our setting, we take $\hat{A}_{k,hw}$ to be given by an
arbitrary attribution method (); we denote this generalized version by RRR*.
In contrast to the loss, only regularizes attributions *outside* the
ground truth masks. While it thus does not introduce a uniformity prior
similar to the loss, it also does not explicitly promote high importance
attributions inside the masks.

func_details.relevant_paper:
GradCam computes importance attributions as a ReLU-thresholded,
gradient-weighted sum of activation maps. In detail, it is given by
$\text{ReLU}(\sum_c \alpha_c^k \odot U_c)$ with $c$ denoting the channel
dimension, and $\alpha^k$ the average-pooled gradients of the output for
class $k$ with respect to the activations $U$ of the last convolutional
layer in the model.

RRR* introduced the RRR loss to regularize the normalized input gradients
$\hat{A}_{k,hw}$ as $$\label{eq:rrr}
    \textstyle \mathcal{L}_{\text{loc},k} = \sum_{h=1}^H\sum_{w=1}^W (1-M_{k,hw}) \hat{A}_{k,hw}^2 \;.$$

arbitrary attribution method (); we denote this generalized version by RRR*.

ground truth masks. While it thus does not introduce a uniformity prior
similar to the loss, it also does not explicitly promote high importance
attributions inside the masks.

func_details.description:
Performs linear map calculations on a batched image tensor to generate gradient-based explanations.

:param in_tensor: A 4D tensor representing batched images with dimensions [batch_size, channels, height, width].
:param idx: Optional parameter. Either a list or tensor of indices 
:param color_explanations: A boolean indicating whether to generate color-coded gradient explanations. Default is True.
:param keep_graph: A boolean indicating whether to retain the computation graph for further gradient calculations. Default is False.

func_details.code_context:
---- explanation_mode (from bcos/models/bcos_common.py) ----
    def explanation_mode(self):
        """
        Creates a context manager which puts model in to explanation
        mode and when exiting puts it into normal mode back again.
        """
        return self._expl_mode_ctx



---- gradient_to_image (from bcos/models/bcos_common.py) ----
    def gradient_to_image(
        cls,
        image: "Tensor",
        linear_mapping: "Tensor",
        smooth: int = 0,
        alpha_percentile: float = 99.5,
    ) -> "np.ndarray":
        # shape of img and linmap is [C, H, W], summing over first dimension gives the contribution map per location
        contribs = (image * linear_mapping).sum(0, keepdim=True)
        contribs = contribs[0]
        # Normalise each pixel vector (r, g, b, 1-r, 1-g, 1-b) s.t. max entry is 1, maintaining direction
        rgb_grad = linear_mapping / (
            linear_mapping.abs().max(0, keepdim=True)[0] + 1e-12
        )
        # clip off values below 0 (i.e., set negatively weighted channels to 0 weighting)
        rgb_grad = rgb_grad.clamp(0)
        # normalise s.t. each pair (e.g., r and 1-r) sums to 1 and only use resulting rgb values
        rgb_grad = cls._to_numpy(rgb_grad[:3] / (rgb_grad[:3] + rgb_grad[3:] + 1e-12))

        # Set alpha value to the strength (L2 norm) of each location's gradient
        alpha = linear_mapping.norm(p=2, dim=0, keepdim=True)
        # Only show positive contributions
        alpha = torch.where(contribs[None] < 0, torch.zeros_like(alpha) + 1e-12, alpha)
        if smooth:
            alpha = F.avg_pool2d(alpha, smooth, stride=1, padding=(smooth - 1) // 2)
        alpha = cls._to_numpy(alpha)
        alpha = (alpha / np.percentile(alpha, alpha_percentile)).clip(0, 1)

        rgb_grad = np.concatenate([rgb_grad, alpha], axis=0)
        # Reshaping to [H, W, C]
        grad_image = rgb_grad.transpose((1, 2, 0))
        return grad_image
